questions.title: How does the 'substantial evidence' standard of review affect an asylum appeal in the Tenth Circuit?
questions.question_body: I'm confused about the standard of review used in Jimenez v. Bondi. The court mentions that findings of fact are reviewed under a 'substantial evidence' standard and are conclusive unless any reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to conclude otherwise. Does this mean the appellate court cannot reconsider the facts even if they find the IJ's logic flawed, as long as there is some evidence in the record to support the conclusion?

questions.title: At what point do threats and psychological harm cross the threshold from 'harassment' to 'persecution'?
questions.question_body: In this case, the court acknowledged that the petitioners suffered death threats and a terrifying encounter with their child, but still ruled that this didn't amount to 'past persecution' because there was no lasting physical harm. If physical violence isn't strictly required, what specific markers is the court looking for to distinguish between 'psychologically unsettling' events and actual persecution?

questions.title: How do courts distinguish between a 'central reason' and a 'tangential reason' in mixed-motive nexus cases?
questions.question_body: The court found that the petitioners' political opinion was 'tangential and subordinate' to the actual reason for the harm (the professional dispute with Don Rafa). However, the persecutors specifically called them 'snitches from Liberal Party.' I don't understand how a threat that explicitly mentions a protected ground (political party) can be dismissed as tangential if the persecutor also has a personal vendetta. How is the 'central reason' test applied when both motives are present?

questions.title: Does a failure to report persecution to the government always defeat the 'unable or unwilling' prong of an asylum claim?
questions.question_body: The court emphasizes that the petitioners didn't report the threats to the government, which undercut their claim that Colombia is unable to protect them. But the petitioners argued that reporting would be futile because the persecutors are aligned with the president. Is there a legal mechanism to prove 'futility' without first reporting the crime, or does the law effectively require a petitioner to risk reporting to the police to prove the police are corrupt?

questions.title: What constitutes 'reasonable' internal relocation if the persecutor has national-level political ties?
questions.question_body: The court suggests that because the petitioners spent three weeks in the Bogota countryside and their father still works for the government, relocation within Colombia is feasible. But if the persecutor (Don Rafa) is aligned with the sitting President of the country, doesn't that imply a level of reach that makes relocation anywhere in the country risky? I'm struggling to see how the court balances the 'reasonableness' of relocation against the political reach of the persecutor.

questions.title: Why does a failure to qualify for asylum automatically result in a denial of Withholding of Removal?
questions.question_body: The conclusion of the opinion states that because the petitioners failed to meet the asylum standards, they 'necessarily fail to meet the higher standard for withholding of removal.' I thought withholding of removal had a different burden of proof (clear probability vs. well-founded fear). Why does the failure of the asylum claim automatically preclude the withholding claim in this instance?
